title: In praise of libraries
text: The public library may be the most quietly {{1}} invention of civic life, and the easiest to take for granted. Before lending libraries, books {{2}} fortunes and reading belonged to those who could pay; a Scottish immigrant called Andrew Carnegie helped {{3}} more than 2,500 of them across the English-speaking world on the theory that anyone who used one could climb. Their deeper business, though, was never only books. A library is {{4}} from the weather, from loneliness, from the noise of the street; it is a study without fees and an office without rent. The librarian who {{5}} a bewildered teenager towards the right shelf performs a service no search engine replicates, and study after study {{6}} what regulars know: loan numbers may wobble, but {{7}} keeps rising, because the need for warm, free, unworried public space does not fade. A city, as the saying goes, ends up with the libraries it {{8}} — and the ones that survive their budget rounds tend to be busier than ever, full of toddlers, teenagers, job applicants and pensioners, all borrowed at the price of nothing at all.

gaps.explanation: 'the most quietly radical invention' — deep-reaching change.
'books cost fortunes' — cost takes the thing as subject.
'helped build more than 2,500' — help is followed by the bare infinitive.
'a refuge from the weather' — a place of safety.
'guides a bewildered teenager towards the right shelf' — leads helpfully.
'study after study confirms' — supports the claim again.
'footfall keeps rising' — the count of people walking in.
'the libraries it deserves' — gets what its care or neglect merits.
